evidence: The hunk calls addEdges(vName, ...) with the bare name for segment-local vars, so same-named locals share one adjacency set. PR #2's eb98f23 diff shows exactly the claimed fix: segment vars keyed only as `${segName}.${vName}` and addVarEdges called with the canonical name, so 'already fixed on main' holds.
guidance_note: When a graph node set holds both a bare and a qualified alias for one declaration, key every node by exactly one canonical name before writing the edge builder.

evidence: The `key` case only checks for a non-empty string, so `cache: { key: "branch" }` yields zero refs and a constant cache key with no error. Closing #1 as superseded does not answer it, because the same loader code moved into #2 and on to main, and nothing in the packet shows this gap addressed there.
guidance_note: Before closing a superseded PR, carry its open review threads over to the PR that absorbed the code, not just the ones already fixed there.

narrative: This PR was superseded by #2, which bundled the same 3rq.1 commit. The agent correctly answered the graph-conflation finding as already fixed on main. It left the cache.key finding unanswered when it closed the PR, even though that code lives on in main.
guidance_observations: Opening #1 and then #2 containing #1's commit split the review of one loader across two PRs, and one thread was dropped when the first PR closed.

evidence: The original comment said locals are referenced as `.<segment>.<var>`, while the loader also accepted bare `.local`. eb98f23 rewrote the comment to document both forms, and added segScope so the loader actually enforces the own-segment-bare / cross-segment-namespaced rule.
guidance_note: When a scoping rule is written in a comment, make the validator enforce that exact rule in the same commit and test each visibility case.

evidence: The agent fixed only the cycle-detector call site and deferred the rest as 'pre-existing code from the 3rq.1 loader foundation — they predate this PR'. That is false relative to master: #1 never merged, so this PR (+2340, it carries the whole loader) introduced every split site. PR #3's summary then had to 'fix dsl-loader path handling for variable names containing dots', which confirms the bug was real.
guidance_note: Check 'pre-existing' against the merge base before deferring a finding; code this PR adds is this PR's to fix, and the reviewer had already listed all four sites.

evidence: eb98f23 added segScope for segment templates and made the cycle graph namespaced-only, but left allVarNames adding bare locals for global templates and depends_on. It also added a comment saying 'depends_on takes explicit fully-qualified names', which the next line contradicts. A bare depends_on now passes cross-ref, but its edge is dropped by `allVarNames.has(dep)` in the graph, so cycles can be missed. The PR merged 4 minutes after this round with the thread unanswered.
guidance_note: When a fix narrows scope rules for one consumer of a shared name set, grep every other consumer of that set (global templates, depends_on, the cycle graph) and make them agree in the same commit.

narrative: The scoping fix in eb98f23 fixed segment templates and the cycle graph, but left the global allVarNames set accepting bare locals. Round 1 caught that mismatch, and the PR merged without addressing it. The split-path finding was half-fixed on a false 'pre-existing' claim, and the next PR redid the work.
guidance_observations: The agent merged with an unanswered round-1 finding on its own fix commit, which turned a known regression into a follow-up.
Deferring to a ticket as 'pre-existing' was used on code this very PR introduced.

evidence: The agent's own resolution concedes that null and absent paths reach the fallback through 'coercion failures (e.g. from a null parent or truly absent path)', so last_error was being recorded on normal events. Accepting was right. The fix's execution, though, suppressed every fallback for every hook field, and it ignored the reviewer's first sentence about the inaccurate comments. That produced F6, F7 and F8.
guidance_note: Before adding a suppress-error flag, list each path that reaches the suppressed call (missing path, null leaf, type mismatch) and each field it applies to, then suppress only the cases that are expected.

evidence: It is true that declareHookDataInputs has no call site. The agent says no runtime path renders DSL templates through SourceRegistry yet, so nothing can fail at render time; the packet does not show the renderer, so that claim is unverified. The cited law answers a question nobody asked: the finding is about wiring, not duplicate definitions.
guidance_note: Don't ship a registration helper without its caller; land the function together with the first consumer that invokes it.

evidence: The file comment says arrays are 'currently always string[] from hook data', but the type said `readonly unknown[]`. a4ff363 narrows it to `readonly string[]`, which matches the documented contract.
guidance_note: When a comment states a narrower contract than the type, narrow the type to match before opening the PR.

evidence: The PR added array branches to typeOf/toString/toNumber/toBool with no tests. a4ff363 adds exactly the requested cases to test/var-store.test.ts.
guidance_note: When you add a variant to a value union, add a test case for that variant to every existing per-variant helper suite in the same commit.

evidence: The hunk returns `raw as readonly unknown[]` after only Array.isArray, so mixed arrays went through unchecked. The resolution validates every element is a string at the trust boundary, which is the check the cited law permits.
guidance_note: At a trust-boundary cast, validate the full declared shape (element types too), not just the outer container.

evidence: F1 opened with 'The comments about null/absent hook-data paths don't match runtime behavior'. The F1 fix added the optional flag but left the comment 'resolvePath returns null (treated as undefined by applyFallback → 0)' unchanged. The agent's own F1 resolution describes null going through coercion failure, which contradicts that comment. The PR was closed minutes later as the wrong approach, so ignoring this cost only the round.
guidance_note: When a finding has two parts (a wrong comment and a behavior bug), fix both in one commit; the comment line was quoted in the original finding.

evidence: The hunk shows `meta.optional` passed to applyFallback inside the coercion catch path. So the F5 trust-boundary throw on a mixed array is now silently swallowed for every hook field, and a malformed payload that used to record last_error no longer does. The PR closed without a reply.
guidance_note: When suppressing errors for 'absent', branch on the raw value (undefined/null) rather than on the field, so type-mismatch coercion errors keep recording.

evidence: The F1 fix passes `optional=true` for every HOOK_DATA_FIELDS entry, including the block the file labels always-present (session_id, cwd). A missing required field now falls back silently where it used to record an error. The PR closed without a reply.
guidance_note: When adding an optional/required flag to a field list, set it per entry from the schema's nullability instead of hard-coding one value in the loop.

narrative: All three findings in round 1 came from the single F1 fix. It ignored the comment half of the finding, suppressed coercion errors along with absence errors, and applied the flag to required fields as well as optional ones. The PR was then abandoned as the wrong approach, so the round bought nothing.
guidance_observations: A blanket boolean flag was used where the fix needed a per-case distinction (absent vs malformed, required vs optional); that one shortcut produced every round-1 finding.
The F1 fix quietly undid the F5 fail-loud trust-boundary check in the same commit, and no test asserted that last_error still records on malformed input.

evidence: `try { fs.unlinkSync(sockPath) } catch {}` followed by a retried listen that exits 0 on EADDRINUSE leaves no daemon and a stale socket, as claimed. The fix (log + shutdown(1)) is right. The defect, though, is a swallowed error, not a null guard.
guidance_note: Treat every empty `catch {}` on a step that a later step depends on as a decision point in the original PR: propagate the error or exit non-zero.

evidence: The hunk's `if (code !== "EEXIST") return "contended"` turns EACCES/ENOTDIR into a spin until the deadline. The fix widened the outcome to held/contended/error. That fix also made every unlink failure fatal, including benign ENOENT, which F22 later caught.
guidance_note: When splitting errors into fatal vs benign, enumerate each errno at each syscall in the function (openSync and unlinkSync both), including ENOENT races.

evidence: The isSocketAlive hunk has done() reachable from connect, error, and the timer with no settled guard. The fix added the guard and clearTimeout, but the agent did not apply clearTimeout back to canConnect, the function it was mirroring (F14).
guidance_note: When fixing a function by copying a sibling's pattern, diff the two afterward and backport whatever the fix added to the sibling.

evidence: The header pointed to rust-client/src/acquire.rs, which does not exist (the review summary lists only main.rs). Both references were corrected.
guidance_note: Grep every file path named in a new comment against the tree before committing.

evidence: obtainDaemonAsync() is called right before process.exit(0), and its first await suspends before spawn, so the daemon never warms. The agent agreed ('always wrong for this caller') and added a synchronous kick with a test proving there is no microtask suspension.
guidance_note: Before replacing a synchronous call with an async one, check whether the caller exits right after; if it does, keep the call synchronous.

evidence: Same defect as F5 at the install URL handler, which also exits afterward. It was fixed by the same switch to obtainDaemonKick.

Rust flock on a persistent `create(true)` file leaves spawn.lock behind, and Node's `openSync("wx")` then reads it as held for up to 10s. Aligning Rust on create_new + unlink is the right fix. The law cited is about type proliferation, though, and does not fit a cross-runtime protocol mismatch.
guidance_note: When two runtimes share a lock file, write down the protocol (acquire, release, stale) once and check both implementations against it before opening the PR.

evidence: The header claimed the runtimes 'agree on socketPath() and spawnLockPath()' while using different lock semantics, which is true and is the F7 bug restated. Even the F4-fixed header still said 'real libc::flock', so this is not caused by the F4 fix.

fs.mkdirSync can throw out of a function typed Promise<ObtainResult>. ensureStateDir converts it to a failed result. The same round's suppressed comment flagged spawnFn throwing too, and that was left for F15.
guidance_note: When fixing a non-throwing-contract violation, list every synchronous call in the function that can throw and wrap them all; the same review had already named spawnFn.

evidence: The agent said: 'obtainDaemonAsync was renamed to obtainDaemonKick in the previous commit; the daemon header comment didn't follow.' After the F5 fix, obtainDaemon() had no call sites, yet the server header still named it.
guidance_note: After renaming or replacing a function in a fix, grep the old name across comments and docs in the same commit.

evidence: The F7 fix removed flock in favor of create_new + unlink, but the Rust header and section comment still said 'flock-gated' and 'flock is the thundering-herd optimization'.
guidance_note: When a fix replaces a mechanism, grep for the old mechanism's name (here 'flock', 'advisory') across the changed files before pushing.

evidence: The F11 fix rewrote the section header but left 'The lock auto-releases when the client process exits (advisory locks vanish on close)' a few lines below. The round-2 summary had already flagged that exact sentence as a suppressed comment. The agent called it the 'last residual flock-era wording'.
guidance_note: When fixing a stale comment, read the whole comment block and the review summary's suppressed comments, not only the anchored line.

evidence: It is true that writeFileSync's mode applies only on create. The impact is overstated, though: the pidfile holds pid, version and binPath, all diagnostic. A one-line chmod is a reasonable accept. single-enforcer has nothing to do with file permissions.

The hunk shows canConnect calling `setTimeout(...).unref()` with no handle. The agent concedes: 'isSocketAlive was fixed for this in round 1 but canConnect was left with the same gap'. That is the very function the F3 fix said it was mirroring.
guidance_note: When a finding says 'do it like sibling X', check X still has the full pattern after your fix and backport anything you added.

evidence: spawnFn() is invoked unguarded in a Promise<ObtainResult> function. The agent said it was the 'same class of contract violation I fixed for fs.mkdirSync', and the round-1 summary had already raised it as a suppressed comment.
guidance_note: When fixing one throw site against a non-throwing contract, audit every call in that function in the same commit.

evidence: The probe-then-unlink race in handleAddressInUse is real. The agent chose the reviewer's 'second liveness check' option, which narrows the window but does not close it. Its claim that the remaining window is the 'gap between stat and unlink' is loose, since the check is an async connect probe, not a stat.
guidance_note: For check-then-destroy races on a shared path, prefer a mechanism that makes the race impossible (a lock or inode compare) over a repeated check.

evidence: STALE_LOCK_MS=10s against totalTimeoutMs=2s means a crashed holder blocks obtain past its deadline. The lockFallbackMs bypass is a sound fix. It was applied only to obtainDaemon, not to obtainDaemonKick or Rust, which led to F18, F19 and F24. The law token does not describe 'the lock is only an optimization'.
guidance_note: When fixing a policy ('the lock must never block availability'), apply it to every entry point that takes the lock (Node obtain, Node kick, Rust kick) in the same commit.

evidence: The kick hunk does `if (lock.kind !== "held") return`, so a lock error is a hard stop. That is the same lock-is-load-bearing gap the F17 fix closed only in obtainDaemon. The agent's reply calls it the 'same dataflow-not-control-flow argument from the previous round, applied to the kick path'.
guidance_note: After establishing an invariant in one function, grep for every caller of the same lock primitive and apply it there too.

evidence: After the F18 fix, the kick still returns silently on 'contended', so a crashed holder blocks warm-up for up to 10s. That is the kick-path analog of F17's lockFallbackMs, which the earlier fixes did not carry over. F18's reviewer had suggested keeping contended as an early return, so this is not an F18 incompleteness.
guidance_note: When adding a crash-recovery path to one lock consumer, enumerate each lock outcome (held, contended, error) at each consumer and decide recovery for every cell.

evidence: isSocketAlive maps the 50ms timeout to `done(false)`, which feeds a destructive unlink. Timeout-means-dead was in the original round-0 isSocketAlive (F3 hunk), so this is not fix-caused. The 3-state probe with unknown treated as alive is the right shape.
guidance_note: When a probe result gates a destructive action, give timeout and unknown their own outcome and map them to the non-destructive branch.

evidence: The test named 'connect fails (ECONNREFUSED)' asserts only EADDRINUSE and unlink+rebind, so the name over-claims. The test was in the original file, so this is not fix-caused. The added connect assertion now covers the probe's dead-code set.
guidance_note: Make each test assert every claim in its name.

evidence: The F2 fix made 'unlink failures during staleness reclaim surface as { kind: "error" }'. The hunk shows that covers ENOENT from a concurrent remover, so obtainDaemon fails spuriously on a benign race. The agent had just added ENOENT tolerance to server.ts's unlink for F20 without sweeping acquire.ts.
guidance_note: When a fix turns a swallowed error into a fatal one, list which errnos are benign races (ENOENT on unlink) and exempt them in the same commit.

evidence: The test 'spawns unlocked when lock acquisition errors' was added by the F18 fix. Its finally block reassigns `process.stderr.write` to a bound copy after mockRestore(), which replaces the restored original with a wrapper.
guidance_note: Use jest.spyOn + mockRestore alone to stub globals in tests; never hand-restore on top of it.

evidence: Rust's try_acquire_spawn_lock returns None for both contention and errors, and the kick treats None as contention. That is the gap F18 and F19 closed only on the Node side; the agent called it the 'same architectural concern as Node thread 7 in the previous round, applied to Rust'. Cross-runtime parity is a real need, but the law token does not name it.
guidance_note: When a lock protocol has a mirror in another runtime, port each change to the mirror in the same commit, as the F7 fix had already established.

evidence: The line-270 test ('surfaces unrecoverable spawn-lock errors') was added by the F2 fix; the line-348 occurrence is the F18-fix test. Saving statSync().mode and later passing it to chmodSync is technically wrong. 'Non-portable' is overstated, since chmod ignores the file-type bits. Masking with 0o7777 is cheap.

`Promise.resolve(fn(...)).finally(...)` evaluates fn before the chain exists, so a synchronous throw skips cleanup, as claimed. withTempState comes from the original test file. Rewriting it as async try/finally is correct.
guidance_note: Write cleanup helpers as async try/finally rather than Promise.resolve(fn()).finally().

evidence: The kick path was added by the F5 fix and its spawn was later extracted into safeSpawn (F18 fix). It calls spawnFn() and discards the boolean, while obtainDaemon treats false as failure. A false return from spawnDaemonDetachedReal (missing argv[1]) was therefore silent.
guidance_note: When a new code path calls an existing function, handle every documented failure signal (throw and false return) that the existing caller handles.

narrative: Fifteen rounds, most of them paying for fixes that landed in one place but not in the place right next to it. Examples: clearTimeout added to isSocketAlive but not to canConnect, the throw contract fixed for mkdir but not for spawn, and the lock-never-blocks-availability policy applied to obtainDaemon, then the Node kick, then the Rust kick, one round each. The flock-to-existence-lock switch cost two more rounds of stale comments. Rounds 2, 4, 6, 9, 10, 11 and 13 trace to fixes from earlier rounds. The original findings (async-before-exit, cross-runtime lock mismatch, probe races) were real and handled well.
guidance_observations: The agent repeatedly admitted the pattern in its own replies ('same class I fixed in round 2', 'left with the same gap', 'same concern applied to Rust') without ever doing a sweep in the fix commit.

Suppressed low-confidence comments in the round summaries (spawnFn throws, the flock-era sentence, the mode mask) predicted the next round's findings; reading them during each fix would have saved rounds.

Law tokens were attached to most fixes even when they did not describe the change (single-enforcer on a chmod, one-type-per-behavior on a cross-runtime protocol), which adds noise without guiding the fix.
